Article 17
Forms of prevention of violence against children and women carried out by PPT, can be implemented through:
a. Socialization activities of laws and regulations to the community related to the protection of the rights of children and women; and

Article 16
(1) In order to provide services and protection to children and women from violence, the Regional Government establishes PPT as an integrated service center for children and women victims of violence.
(2) PPT as referred to in paragraph (1), consists of elements from the Health Office, Youth Education and Sports Office, Social Office, Cooperatives Industry and Trade Office, Population and Civil Registration Office, Women Empowerment and Family Planning Agency, Community Empowerment Agency, Civil Service Police Unit, Regional General Hospital, Police Resort, Non-Governmental Organizations, and Universities.
(3) PPT as referred to in paragraph (2), shall be established by Regent's decree.
(4) The provision of services to victims shall be carried out in an integrated manner by PPT.
(5) PPT as referred to in paragraph (4) may receive and send case referrals from or to other service units in a networked manner.
(6) PPT provides services and temporary protection in the form of safe houses.
(7) In the event that PPT does not yet have a safe house, then victims of violence shall be referred to PPT that has a safe house.
(8) PPT consists of several counseling fields.
(9) The counseling fields as referred to in paragraph (8) shall at minimum consist of:
a. legal field;
b. health field;
c. spiritual field; and
d. psychology field.
(10) Further provisions regarding the organizational structure of PPT shall be regulated by Regent's Regulation.

Article 9
Exploitation as referred to in Article 4 letter e is caused by:
a. acts that exploit economically or sexually with the intention of benefiting oneself or others;
b. acts with or without the consent of the victim which include but are not limited to prostitution, forced labor or services, slavery or similar practices, oppression, extortion, exploitation of physical, sexual, reproductive organs, or unlawfully removing or transplanting organs and/or body tissues or exploiting the labor or capabilities of a person by other parties to obtain benefits either material or immaterial; and/or
c. all forms of exploitation of sexual organs or other body organs of the victim to obtain benefits, including but not limited to all activities of prostitution or sexual abuse.

6.2.rationale: The original regulation discusses "eksploitasi" (Pasal 4 huruf e; Pasal 9) and includes examples like prostitution, forced labor/services, slavery-like practices, etc. It also cites the national anti-trafficking law in the 'Mengingat' section. However, nowhere does it explicitly identify or provide specific measures for "korban perdagangan orang" (trafficking victims) as a distinct intersectional group; it treats exploitation as one form of violence generally. The judge inferred trafficking coverage from the broad exploitation definition, but the indicator appears to require explicit mention/targeting of trafficking victims. Since the retrieved passages contained only general exploitation language (not trafficking-victim-specific provisions), the 'Yes' conclusion is an overreach.

6.8.rationale: The Indonesian text provides general legal assistance for victims and mentions services for "pelapor, dan saksi" (Pasal 3 ayat (1) huruf d) and "Pelayanan hukum" to help victims through legal processes (Pasal 19 huruf d), plus rights to "pendampingan psikologis dan hukum" (Pasal 10 huruf f). But it does not specifically address women involved in legal processes as an intersectional category (e.g., women defendants/detainees, women in custody, or special protections for women navigating justice processes beyond being victims/witnesses/reporters). The judge treated general victim legal aid and witness/reporter services as satisfying the indicator, which likely expects explicit coverage of women’s legal-process involvement as a vulnerable group. The information in candidates supports general legal services, not the more specific intersectional criterion, so the 'Yes' is due to overly broad interpretation.
